title: Crossair 498
summary: The aircraft departed Zurich at 5:54 PM on standard instrument departure SID ZUE 1Y but the crew made incorrect entries without full coordination. The aircraft turned right instead of following the approved left turn path. When ATC queried the right turn, the pilot responded "Stand by" and lost radio contact. At 5:56 PM, 116 seconds into flight, the aircraft disappeared from radar in a diving right spiral turn. The pilot had traces of benzodiazepine sedative in his system and had lost spatial orientation.
probable_cause: The commander lost spatial orientation and entered a spiral dive to the right. Inappropriate crew priorities, incomplete SID entry, and the commander's cognitive state from benzodiazepine drug traces contributed to the loss of control.

factors.evidence: commander took the aircraft into a spiral dive to the right because, with a probability bordering on certainty, he had lost spatial orientation

commander dispensed with use of the autopilot under instrument flight conditions and during the work-intensive climb phase of the flight
first officer took only inadequate measures to prevent or recover from the spiral dive
aircraft went into a diving right turn and disappeared from radar screens 116 seconds into flight

events.text: Aircraft departed Runway 28 heading west at 5:54 PM CEST, cleared for standard instrument departure SID ZUE 1Y

Aircraft disappeared from radar screens in diving right turn and crashed into field 5 km northwest of Zurich runway, igniting over 2000 kg jet fuel

title: 2000 Marsa Brega Short 360 crash
operator: Avisto Air Service (chartered by Sirte Oil)
summary: A Swiss-registered Short 360 en route from Tripoli to Marsa Brega encountered icing conditions in mid-flight. The de-icing device had not been activated by the crew. Ice accumulated and melted, flooding both engines. The left engine failed at 11:36 UTC, followed shortly by the right engine. With both engines inoperative, the crew ditched the aircraft into the Mediterranean Sea. The pilots were distracted by unrelated conversations and were not aware of the deteriorating aircraft condition until too late.
probable_cause: The probable cause was the de-icing device not being activated, allowing the aircraft to fly into icing conditions where ice accumulated, melted and flooded both engines. Contributing factors were crew distraction by unrelated conversations and inadequate weather briefing comprehension.

title: Kenya Airways 431
summary: Kenya Airways Flight 431 crashed into the Atlantic Ocean shortly after takeoff from Abidjan on 30 January 2000 at night. The crew responded to a false stall warning by pushing the control column forward, placing the aircraft into an unintended descent. The GPWS warnings were masked by priority stall and overspeed warnings in conditions with no external visual references. The Commission of Inquiry concluded the pilot applied stall recovery procedure while the airplane was not in a true stall situation.
probable_cause: The crash was caused by the pilot flying applying one part of the procedure, by pushing forward on the control column to stop the stick shaker, following the initiation of a stall warning on rotation, while the airplane was not in a true stall situation. The pilot flying's action on the control column put the airplane into a descent without the crew realizing it. The GPWS warnings were masked by priority stall and overspeed warnings. The conditions for takeoff towards the sea at night provided no external visual references.

factors.evidence: Just seconds after takeoff, at the moment when the first officer requested the landing gear to be retracted, the stall warning sounded in the cockpit.
The pilot flying told the captain to silence the stall warning and put the aircraft into a controlled descent.
The GPWS warnings could have alerted the crew to an imminent contact with the sea were masked by the priority stall and overspeed warnings
the conditions for a takeoff performed towards the sea and at night provided no external visual references
The aircraft crashed into the Atlantic Ocean
The airframe was completely destroyed by the impact.

events.text: Just seconds after takeoff, at the moment when the first officer requested the landing gear to be retracted, the stall warning sounded in the cockpit.
The first officer told the captain to silence the stall warning and the aircraft was put into a controlled descent.

The aircraft crashed into the Atlantic Ocean, 2 km east of the airport, off the Ivory Coast.

title: Alaska Airlines 261

route.from_name: Licenciado Gustavo Díaz Ordaz International Airport

location.name: Pacific Ocean near Anacapa Island, California

summary: Alaska Airlines Flight 261, a McDonnell Douglas MD-83 flying from Puerto Vallarta toward Seattle with a stop in San Francisco, suffered a catastrophic loss of pitch control on 31 January 2000 after the horizontal stabilizer trim system's jackscrew assembly failed from worn acme nut threads, and crashed into the Pacific Ocean near Anacapa Island, California, while diverting to Los Angeles. The crew struggled for over two hours with a jammed stabilizer, and when they finally freed it using the primary trim system, it moved to an extreme nose-down position, forcing the aircraft into a nosedive from about 31,050 ft. The NTSB attributed the crash to inadequate maintenance that allowed excessive jackscrew wear, killing all 88 aboard.
probable_cause: The NTSB determined the probable cause to be a loss of airplane pitch control resulting from the in-flight failure of the horizontal stabilizer trim system jackscrew assembly's Acme nut threads, the excessive wear of which resulted from Alaska Airlines' insufficient lubrication of the jackscrew assembly.

factors.evidence: Inadequate maintenance led to excessive wear and eventual failure of a critical flight control system during flight.
A loss of airplane pitch control resulting from the in-flight failure of the horizontal stabilizer trim system jackscrew assembly's Acme nut threads.
Alaska Airlines dispatch personnel appear to have attempted to influence the flight crew to continue to San Francisco instead of diverting to Los Angeles.
Upon being freed, the stabilizer quickly moved to an extreme 'nose-down' position, forcing the aircraft into a nosedive, and both pilots struggled together to regain control.
The plane dropped from about 31,050 ft to between 23,000 ft and lower in around 80 seconds.

events.text: Flight 261 departed Puerto Vallarta at 13:37 PST and climbed to its intended cruising altitude of flight level 310 (31,000 ft).

Before 15:49, the flight crew contacted dispatch and maintenance-control to discuss a jammed horizontal stabilizer and a possible diversion, but Alaska Airlines dispatch personnel appear to have attempted to influence the crew to continue to San Francisco.

At 16:09, the flight crew successfully used the primary trim system to unjam the stuck horizontal stabilizer, but upon being freed it quickly moved to an extreme nose-down position, forcing the aircraft into a nosedive.
The plane dropped from about 31,050 ft to between 23,000 ft and lower in around 80 seconds as both pilots struggled together to regain control of the aircraft.

title: Air Philippines 541
summary: Flight 541 approached Davao City behind a Philippine Airlines Airbus A320. When the crew observed the preceding aircraft had not cleared the runway, they advised ATC and initiated a missed approach. Instead of climbing to 4,000 ft on instruments and circling as procedure requires, the pilots attempted visual flight at low altitude in instrument conditions. The aircraft struck a coconut tree 500 ft above sea level.
probable_cause: The pilots attempted to fly under visual flight rules in instrument meteorological conditions at a lower than required altitude, resulting in controlled flight into terrain.

title: Wuhan Airlines 343
summary: Wuhan Airlines Flight 343, a Xian Y-7, crashed on 22 June 2000 while attempting to land at Wuhan Wangjiadun Airport during severe weather. The aircraft circled the airport for 30 minutes in thunderstorm conditions with 451 thunderclaps in 10 minutes. The crew debated diverting but the captain decided to continue the approach. The aircraft was struck by lightning and encountered windshear, becoming uncontrollable. The fuselage broke into two sections; all 38 passengers and 4 crew were killed, along with 7 people on the ground.
probable_cause: The aircraft was struck by lightning and encountered windshear while attempting to land during severe thunderstorm conditions. The crew and ATC both violated standard operating procedures for severe weather, and the captain made an incorrect decision to continue the approach rather than divert to an alternate airport.

title: Alliance Air 7412
summary: The Boeing 737 entered a stall while on approach to Patna at high altitude. The crew, flying above the usual approach altitude and turning to the left, experienced stick shaker activation but continued to bank while losing altitude. The aircraft crashed in a residential area behind Gardani Bagh Girls School. Investigation found the crew made high-pitch attitude maneuvers with engines at idle and elected to execute a go-around instead of stall recovery.
probable_cause: Pilot error: the aircraft was on approach with engines at idle thrust, crew made several high-pitch attitude maneuvers, and when stall warning sounded they elected to execute go-around procedure instead of proper stall recovery, causing actual stall condition.

title: Air France 4590
summary: Air France Flight 4590 ran over debris on the runway dropped by a preceding Continental Airlines DC-10, causing a tyre to explode and disintegrate during takeoff at 185 mph. Tyre fragments struck the underside of the Concorde wing, damaging the landing gear and rupturing the integral fuel tank. Large amounts of fuel leaked and ignited, causing loss of thrust in engines 1 and 2. The aircraft lifted off but the loss of thrust, high drag from extended landing gear, and fire damage to flight controls made it impossible to maintain control. The Concorde crashed into a hotel in Gonesse two minutes after takeoff.
probable_cause: A titanium alloy wear strip dropped by the preceding DC-10 caused the Concorde tyre to explode, tyre fragments ruptured the fuel tank, and the ensuing fire disabled engines and flight controls.

title: Gulf Air 072
summary: Gulf Air Flight 072, an Airbus A320-212 flying from Cairo to Bahrain, crashed into the shallow waters of the Persian Gulf 2 km from the airport on 23 August 2000, minutes after a go-around from a failed approach to Runway 12. The captain suffered spatial disorientation, applying a large nose-down input that produced a 15-degree dive; as the aircraft descended, the crew disregarded the GPWS 'sink rate' and 'Whoop, whoop, pull up' warnings while debating flap configuration instead. The Airbus struck the sea at 280 knots, killing all 143 people on board.
probable_cause: The final report found non-adherence to Standard Operating Procedures and loss of spatial and situational awareness by the crew during the approach and go-around, compounded by deficient CRM training at Gulf Air and safety oversight failures by the civil aviation authority.

factors.evidence: The flight crew suffered from spatial disorientation during the go-around and crashed into the shallow waters of the Persian Gulf.
Non-adherence to a number of Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) by the aircraft crew during the approach and final phases of the flight.
Systemic factors also contributed to the accident, including deficiency in crew resource management (CRM) training by Gulf Air.

Flying with a speed of 280 knots and a nose-down pitch of 6.5 degrees, the aircraft slammed onto the sea below, instantly killing all 143 passengers and crew members.

events.text: Captain Shakeeb applied a large nose-down input, inducing a rapid descent at a pitch angle of approximately 15 degrees, the maximum permissible, as the aircraft continued to accelerate under TO/GA thrust.

As the aircraft descended toward the sea, the GPWS escalated to 'Whoop, whoop! Pull up!' while the crew continued discussing flap position as the aircraft descended unchecked.
At 19:30, flying at 280 knots with a nose-down pitch of 6.5 degrees, the aircraft slammed onto the sea, instantly killing all 143 passengers and crew members.

title: Singapore Airlines 006
summary: During heavy rain from Typhoon Xangsane with poor visibility, the aircraft was cleared for takeoff but lined up on the closed runway 05R instead of the assigned runway 05L. The pilots did not see construction equipment on the closed runway and collided with excavators and other machinery after 41 seconds at full throttle. The aircraft broke apart and caught fire, destroying the forward fuselage section. The accident exposed systemic failures including the lack of ground radar, absence of physical barriers or hazard markings on the closed runway, and active taxiway lighting that guided pilots into the construction zone.
probable_cause: The flight crew lined up on the wrong runway due to poor visibility and turned 215 meters too soon. However, the investigation found that ATC cleared takeoff without operational ground radar and the airport lacked proper physical barriers and hazard markings on the closed runway.

title: 2000 ASA Pesada Antonov An-24 crash
summary: On 15 November 2000, an Antonov An-24 operated by ASA Pesada crashed shortly after taking off from Quatro de Fevereiro Airport in Luanda, Angola, banking left before hitting a field in the Golfe II district and exploding; all 57 aboard were killed. A preliminary investigation found the crash was caused by engine failure and also cited ASA Pesada for negligence in failing to keep accurate records of the fuel quantity and passenger numbers on board.
